entries.title: Deep learning grading of Schistosoma japonicum-associated liver fibrosis from ultrasound images: a weighted soft-voting ensemble of convolutional and transformer networks
entries.abstract:
BackgroundDespite progress towards schistosomiasis elimination in China, Schistosoma japonicum-associated liver fibrosis remains a source of morbidity. Ultrasound grading is subjective, and experienced sonographers are scarce in endemic counties.

MethodsWe developed a deep learning ensemble to grade fibrosis from a single B-mode ultrasound image without manual region-of-interest delineation. We analysed 2,921 images from 2,921 adults (aged 18-88 years; median age 54; 46.4% female) at a schistosomiasis hospital in Jiangxi Province, China (2019-2023). Grades 0, 1, 2 and 3 accounted for 12.9%, 34.6%, 32.4% and 20.2% of images, respectively. Reference grades were derived from clinical ultrasound records and radiologist reassessment using the Chinese Handbook of Schistosomiasis Control, with disagreements resolved by consensus. Predictions from ResNet-18, EfficientNet-B0, DenseNet-121 and Swin-T were combined by validation-weighted soft voting. Performance was evaluated on a held-out test set of 440 images.

ResultsThe ensemble achieved a macro-F1 of 0.8527 (95% CI 0.8184-0.8856), accuracy of 0.8500 (95% CI 0.8136-0.8818) and quadratic weighted kappa of 0.9187 (95% CI 0.8983-0.9373) for four-grade classification, outperforming each individual network in macro-F1. All ensemble misclassifications involved adjacent grades. For detecting significant fibrosis (grades 2-3; test-set prevalence 53.0%), sensitivity was 0.9700, specificity 0.9179, positive predictive value 0.9300, negative predictive value 0.9645 and AUROC 0.9817.

ConclusionsThis single-image approach may assist automated grading of S. japonicum-associated liver fibrosis in endemic settings. External validation is needed before clinical implementation.

entries.title: Machine Learning Validation Pipelines: From Tabular Benchmarking to Conformal Calibration and Execution-Grounded Agentic Testing
entries.abstract: Machine learning systems are increasingly required to be multi-layered for software engineering validation protocols, and multiple checks are imposed instead of just one. Many important failure modes, such as deep class imbalance, poor probability calibration, ungrounded execution, and ”attributional” issues, come to a head in low-level deployments, such as automated code generation, credit underwriting, and clinical triage, where failures can be devastating. In clinical triage, credit underwriting, and the automated generation of code situations that are of a high stakes regularly show up critical failure modes such as severe class imbalance, poor probability calibration, unfaithful attribution, and ungrounded execution, for which standard k-fold cross-validation and regularized baselines are entirely inadequate. By combining the findings from 41 empirical studies, this review identifies three main levels of architecture: data leakage prevention and baseline benchmarking (Level 1), post-hoc interpretability audits and glass-box comparisons (Level 2), and distribution-free uncertainty quantification (Level 3). It is particularly important to note that a meta-analysis of 297 financial machine learning papers reveals a general disregard for diagnosis; only 7.1% of the papers examined included Remove and Retrain (ROAR) benchmarks for testing the faithfulness of the explanations, whereas 93.9% used TreeSHAP for feature attribution. The existence of multi-tier verification frameworks is especially important in order to prevent silent failure modes in safetycritical software systems, as these findings demonstrate. Class-conditional Mondrian conformal calibration answers the Minority Coverage Collapse Theorem, recovering +61.7 percentage points of minority coverage (p < 10 −80 ), and pairs with conformalized quantile regression and cost-optimal selective human deferral (θ ∗ = ch/CFN). Layer 4 is pre-deployment gating: on models above 0.85 AUROC, where static toolkits report nothing amiss, the RISED framework surfaces decision threshold-flip rates of 49.1% to 64.2% under minor input perturbations. Layer 5 covers execution-grounded multi-agent verification: closed-loop Abstract Syntax Tree validation with transactional rollback (ExecuGraph), lightweight multi-vector screening (TriEval), arity-matched action fairness auditing (AgentFairBench), and prompt-sensitivity benchmarking of the LLM judges such pipelines rely on to score free-form output (JudgeSense). We then formalize how the layers couple, and set out the order in which they should run.

entries.title: REG2024: a benchmark challenge and curated dataset for pathology report generation from giga- pixel whole-slide images of bladder cancer
entries.abstract: Background We aimed to construct a curated whole-slide image (WSI)-report dataset for bladder cancer and establish a clinically grounded benchmark for evaluating vision–language models through an open community challenge. Methods We curated a dataset of 902 deidentified bladder cancer WSIs paired with corresponding pathology reports. Seven teams submitted distinct modeling frameworks. Performance was assessed using a clinically weighted composite metric integrating word-overlap scores (ROUGE-L, BLEU-4), keyword matching, and embedding-based semantic similarity. Expert mean opinion scores (MOS) were obtained, and the correlation between the weighted-sum score and expert-assigned MOS was analyzed. Results Two modeling strategies emerged: end-to-end generative architectures and multi-step classification-then-generation pipelines. Among individual submissions, the top-ranked multi-step pipeline achieved the highest main-diagnosis accuracy (48/50), whereas end-to-end models showed greater sensitivity to rare pathological features. The weighted-sum metric correlated strongly with MOS within each team (Spearman’s ρ, 0.65–0.91) and, on reports with clinically important misclassifications, agreed with MOS more closely than any single metric. Conclusions Performance variability was influenced by architectural design and the integration of pretrained foundation models. Our proposed evaluation framework addressed key limitations of conventional natural language processing metrics in evaluating pathology reports. This challenge establishes a benchmark for clinical-grade pathology report generation by providing vision-language pathology datasets and introducing a clinically aligned evaluation framework, thereby advancing computational pathology.
